item.title: NBR extends VAT return submission deadline to October 25
item.description:
The National Board of Revenue (NBR) has extended the deadline for submitting online VAT returns for the three tax periods from July to September in its e-VAT system.
Taxpayers can now file these returns without any interest or penalties until October 25.
This decision was announced in a notification issued on Thursday (October 15), signed by Sheikh Md Masudur Rahman, second secretary of the NBR (VAT: Monitoring, Statistics, and Coordination).
The notification stated that following amendments to the VAT return submission regulations at the end of every three tax periods in the National Budget 2026–27, the Value Added Tax and Supplementary Duty (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026 was promulgated.
As a result of incorporating the provision to submit VAT returns after each three-tax-period cycle, certain administrative reforms were required within the e-VAT system.
In this context, in the public interest, the NBR—exercising powers granted under Sub-section (2) of Section 64 of the Value Added Tax and Supplementary Duty Act, 2012—has extended the deadline for submitting online returns for the July–September 2026 tax periods without interest or penalty until October 25.
Meanwhile, the government has issued a new ordinance establishing deadlines for submitting Value Added Tax (VAT) returns.
Under the new provisions, standard registered, enlisted, registrable, or enlistable entities must submit their returns within 15 days following the end of a tax period.
However, government, semi-government, and autonomous organizations, banks, insurance companies, and entities filing nil-returns will have up to 20 days to submit their returns.
The "Value Added Tax and Supplementary Duty (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026" was officially published in an extra edition of the Bangladesh Gazette on October 14.

item.title: Govt borrows Tk24,245cr from banks in Q1 of FY27
item.description:
The government tapped the banking sector for Tk24,245 crore during the first quarter of FY27, underscoring its expanding reliance on bank credit amidst sluggish tax revenues.
This net borrowing throughout the July–September period represents a stark shift from the Tk6,926 crore in net debt repayments made over the same period in FY26, based on Bangladesh Bank figures.
During these three months, public borrowing comprised Tk1,017 crore drawn directly from the central bank alongside Tk23,227 crore secured from commercial lenders.
In FY26, total government bank borrowing reached Tk131,000 crore, eclipsing its official annual target of Tk104,000 crore and rising sharply above the Tk72,372 crore borrowed in FY25.
For FY27, official plans set the bank borrowing threshold at Tk112,000 crore.
Cumulative public debt owed to the domestic banking system crossed the Tk700,000 crore mark as of September 30.
The accelerating credit uptake reflects a persistent shortfall between state revenue generation and spending commitments.
Authorities depend heavily on bank loans to fund infrastructure projects, welfare initiatives, public sector payrolls, and operational expenses, as revenue generation continues to lag behind outlay requirements.
Bangladesh Bank’s monetary policy statement covering July–December 2026 highlighted that government financing shifted heavily toward commercial lenders after the central bank halted automated debt creation (devolvement), while intake through National Savings Certificates also rebounded.
This mounting reliance on commercial banks raises concerns regarding the government's capacity to fund operations without squeezing out credit to private enterprises.
Commercial financial institutions may favor allocating capital to government treasury bills and bonds—which carry minimal default risk—rather than extending credit to businesses in an environment of elevated default risks and broader economic uncertainty.
Private sector credit growth slowed to a mere 4.7% in August 2026, indicating subdued corporate investment appetite alongside constraints on lenders' balance sheet capacity.
Additional crowding-out pressure from public borrowing threatens to restrict capital available for corporate expansion, industrial output, and job creation, potentially dampening overall economic recovery.
However, the liquidity impact remains uneven across the sector.
Institutions holding surplus liquidity can readily expand their government securities portfolios, whereas distressed lenders continue to struggle under severe liquidity constraints.
Consequently, state borrowing needs risk escalating interbank competition for deposits across an already fragile banking industry.
Direct borrowing from Bangladesh Bank carries distinct inflationary risks whenever it expands the monetary base and total money supply without generating a corresponding increase in real economic output.
While borrowing from commercial banks does not exert the same immediate expansionary impact on money supply, it directly crowds out private sector borrowers.
Strains on public finances could escalate further if international fuel and commodity import costs jump due to conflict in the Middle East, driving up state subsidies and borrowing requirements.
Curtailing this structural dependence will necessitate aggressive revenue mobilization, modernized tax administration, and stricter fiscal discipline over public expenditure, according to independent economists.

item.title: National Bank starts repaying its depositors
item.description:
National Bank restarted routine banking operations on Thursday, enabling general depositors to withdraw cash according to their requirements.
The bank began processing deposit payouts for clients who submitted withdrawal requests over the preceding four days.
According to sources within National Bank, the distressed lender secured Tk7,000 crore in liquidity support to resume regular functions. State-run Sonali Bank provided these funds backed by a central bank guarantee.
Bangladesh Bank has applied strict guidelines regarding how National Bank may deploy the capital.
A primary stipulation prohibits using these funds to settle deposits belonging to present or former bank directors, nor can the money be disbursed as loans.
The central bank outlined these directives in a official communication sent to National Bank’s managing director on Monday.
The notice specified that the liquidity assistance carries a 10% interest rate with a maturity period of three months.
In the interim, the lender gathered cash withdrawal requests from clients between October 11 and 14 to gauge overall liquidity demand.
National Bank sources indicated that roughly 11,000 customers applied to withdraw a combined total of Tk2,000 crore across those four days.
Branches nationwide submitted their depositors' requests to the head office, which subsequently supplied the necessary cash.
As an initial measure, the bank was directed to clear withdrawal requests from savings and current account holders over the coming days, with other client categories receiving payouts in later phases.
11 conditions
National Bank must adhere to 11 central bank conditions governing the usage of these funds raised under the central bank guarantee to satisfy depositor claims.
Among these rules, the bank cannot declare cash dividends until the assistance package is fully repaid.
Furthermore, the money cannot be channeled toward loans or investments for current or former directors, or any entities connected to them.
The capital must not be used to refund deposits registered to past or present directors—whether directly or via indirect channels—nor can it back new credit approvals or increase existing credit facilities.
Even previously sanctioned but undisbursed loan amounts cannot be released using this liquidity.
Bangladesh Bank additionally barred using the capital to settle existing interbank obligations or placements, buy out loans or investment portfolios from peer banks, or purchase foreign currency to meet letter of credit obligations linked to forced loans or loans against trust receipts (LTRs).
Depositing the funds into other financial institutions is likewise forbidden.
For the duration of the guarantee, all newly mobilized deposits must be allocated exclusively toward improving the bank's overall liquidity and fulfilling commitments to general depositors.
Operating costs cannot grow by more than 5% year-over-year, and the guaranteed capital cannot be applied toward administrative or operational expenditures.
National Bank is required to submit weekly usage reports to the central bank detailing how the funds are deployed.
Data from National Bank indicates that as of October 12, total deposits stood at Tk33,515 crore, while outstanding loans reached Tk43,230 crore. This resulted in an advance-to-deposit ratio (ADR) of 132%.
Under Bangladesh Bank regulations, commercial banks may lend up to Tk87 for every Tk100 in deposits, placing the maximum allowable ADR ceiling at 87%. By the end of June, nearly 66% of National Bank’s total loan portfolio was classified as non-performing loans.
Latest accounting figures reveal that National Bank’s cumulative borrowings from Bangladesh Bank and other financial institutions—including funds secured through central bank guarantees—total approximately Tk26,000 crore.
Sikder Group held management control over National Bank from 2009 through 2023. Extensive financial irregularities during this timeframe caused substantial losses, pushing the institution into acute financial distress.

item.title: Shama stresses climate justice, accountability ahead of COP31
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam on Thursday highlighted the importance of climate justice and accountability, the loss and damage fund, a just transition and green growth for Bangladesh ahead of COP31.
Speaking at a meeting on Bangladesh’s priorities and preparations for the climate conference, she called for implementing the National Action Plan and ensuring the predictable, adequate and transparent disbursement of global climate finance in line with national priorities.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs hosted the meeting with climate experts and other stakeholders, with the state minister in the chair.
Prime Minister’s Special Assistant on Environment, Forest and Climate Change Md Saimum Parvez, prominent climate experts of Bangladesh, representatives of research organizations, national and international organizations, and senior foreign ministry officials attended the meeting.
Discussions focused on the COP31 action agenda, Bangladesh’s priorities and preparations for the conference.
Shama said the Conference of the Parties (COP) provides a global platform for climate diplomacy, covering adaptation, mitigation and resilience.
She also highlighted the importance of linking the circular economy with green industry and said Bangladesh’s jute, a sustainable and biodegradable natural fibre, will be showcased at COP31.
The state minister urged stakeholders to contribute from their respective positions to strengthen Bangladesh’s stance at the conference.
The participants welcomed the ministry’s initiative, while climate experts shared their perspectives on the COP31 agenda to help shape Bangladesh’s position.
Youth representatives, who are set to participate in the conference for the first time, also shared their views, expectations and proposals to strengthen the country’s preparations.
The participants also mentioned that strategies and policies should be formulated in a holistic way so that they can be implemented beyond COP31.
They also underscored the importance of highlighting flagship projects/initiatives of the government to the world.
COP31 is going to take place in Antalya, Türkiye on November 9-20, 2026.
A Bangladeshi delegation is expected to participate in high-level sessions, negotiations and discussions.
Bangladesh also plans to present its climate priorities and achievements, with a particular focus on showcasing jute products and technology, along with the fibre’s commercial potential as a sustainable alternative to plastic.

item.title: Load-shedding worsens in 21 southwestern districts, deficit hits 116MW
item.description:
Load-shedding has intensified across 21 districts in southwestern Bangladesh, including Khulna, with the power deficit reaching 116 megawatts (MW) during peak hours on Wednesday evening.
The shortage stood at 101MW during the afternoon, leaving residents grappling with frequent and prolonged power cuts.
Belal Hossain, a resident of Goborchaka in Khulna, told Dhaka Tribune that the situation had deteriorated compared with Tuesday.
“Previously, we experienced power cuts for an hour at a time. On Wednesday, outages lasted up to one and a half hours at a stretch. We are now facing 13–14 hours of load-shedding a day,” he said.
Ambia Khatun, a resident of Boyra, said frequent power cuts had compounded the hardship caused by the ongoing gas shortage.
“Gas supply is already severely disrupted, and we are trying to cope by using electricity. Frequent load-shedding has made the situation even more unbearable,” she said.
Latika Rani of Tutpara also reported a sudden deterioration in the power supply, saying outages often occurred even when electricity was urgently needed.
According to the central control room of the West Zone Power Distribution Company Ltd (WZPDCL), electricity demand across its 21-district service area stood at 694MW on Wednesday evening, against a supply of 578MW, leaving a deficit of 116MW.
In the Khulna zone, demand was 528MW, while supply stood at 447MW, resulting in a shortfall of 81MW. In the Barisal zone, demand was 166MW against a supply of 131MW, leaving a deficit of 35MW.
District-wise figures showed load-shedding of 29MW in Khulna, 4MW in Magura, 3MW in Narail, 11MW in Jhenaidah, 2MW in Chuadanga, 1MW in Meherpur, 12MW in Faridpur, 13MW in Rajbari, 4MW in Madaripur, 1MW each in Gopalganj and Shariatpur, 22MW in Barisal, 2MW each in Pirojpur and Jhalakathi, 3MW in Patuakhali, 2MW in Barguna and 4MW in Bhola.
At around 1:00pm on Wednesday, demand across the 21 districts stood at 661MW, while supply was 560MW, leaving a shortfall of 101MW.
In the Khulna zone, demand was 481MW against a supply of 422MW, resulting in a deficit of 59MW. In the Barisal zone, demand stood at 180MW, while supply was 138MW, leaving a shortfall of 42MW.
Afternoon figures showed load-shedding of 17MW in Khulna, 6MW in Magura, 1MW in Narail, 7MW in Jhenaidah, 1MW in Bheramara, 7MW in Kushtia, 10MW in Rajbari, 5MW in Madaripur, 3MW in Gopalganj, 2MW in Shariatpur, 25MW in Barisal, 3MW each in Pirojpur and Jhalakathi, 5MW in Patuakhali, and 3MW each in Barguna and Bhola.
The situation was comparatively better on Tuesday, October 13. At 1:00pm, demand across the 21 districts stood at 741MW against a supply of 705MW, leaving a deficit of 36MW. In the Khulna zone, demand was 567MW and supply 531MW, while the Barisal zone met its full demand of 174MW.
By 7pm, the overall deficit had risen to 79MW, with demand at 721MW and supply at 642MW. In the Khulna zone, demand stood at 551MW against a supply of 504MW, leaving a shortfall of 47MW. In the Barisal zone, demand was 170MW, while supply stood at 138MW, resulting in a deficit of 32MW.

item.title: Dhaka calls for inclusive, results-driven CICA
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir on Thursday reaffirmed Bangladesh's commitment to advance regional cooperation among the Asian countries.
While speaking at the plenary session of the 7th Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) in Baku, the state minister conveyed Bangladesh's full support for CICA's transformation into a full-fledged international regional organization with a clear legal status, a strengthened Secretariat, predictable financing and effective decision-making.
In his statement, he put forward three concrete proposals on the implementation of results-oriented sectoral projects backed by formal follow-up mechanisms to build meaningful partnerships among member states, organizing more in-person events to foster wider stakeholder participation, strengthening exchanges among member states' ICT institutions and developing confidence-building measures for a safe, open and trusted digital space to address emerging challenges in ICT and AI.
This year, the 7th CICA summit is taking place under the chairmanship of Azerbaijan with the theme "A Stronger CICA: Connectivity, Digitalization, and Sustainable Growth in Asia," reflects priorities of vital importance to the peoples of Asia.
During the summit, Lao PDR became the 29th member of this Pan-Asian forum established in 1999 with a view to promoting peace, security and stability across ASIA.
The summit also endorsed the Chairmanship of Azerbaijan for 2026-28 and the appointment of Sultan Hajiyev as the next Secretary General of CICA.
Meanwhile, Bangladesh staged a walkout during the Israeli president's address at the seventh summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) in Baku.
The Bangladesh delegation, led by State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir, walked out of the conference hall as the Israeli president began delivering his speech at the summit, said the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Representatives of several other countries also joined the walkout, boycotting the Israeli president's address.
The delegations left the conference hall in protest during the Israeli president's speech.
The seventh CICA summit is being held in the Azerbaijani capital, bringing together leaders and senior representatives of participating countries to discuss regional cooperation, security and confidence-building measures across Asia.

item.title: Bangladesh ranks 84th in Global Hunger Index 2026
item.description:
Bangladesh ranked 84th in the Global Hunger Index (GHI) 2026, scoring 19.2 and remaining in the “moderate” hunger category, as child undernutrition continues to pose a significant public health challenge despite progress in reducing stunting over the past 2 decades.
The index shows that 8.2% of Bangladesh’s population is undernourished, while 24% of children under 5 suffer from stunting, or low height for their age.
Another 12.9% of children under 5 experience wasting, or low weight for their height, and 3% of children die before reaching the age of 5.
Bangladesh performed better than India and Pakistan but lagged behind Nepal in the regional comparison.
India ranked 100th with a score of 24.1, while Pakistan placed 106th with 25.5, putting both countries in the “serious” hunger category. Nepal ranked 72nd with a score of 14.5, remaining in the “moderate” category.
A lower GHI score indicates lower levels of hunger and undernutrition, although rankings also depend on the performance of other countries included in the assessment.
One of Bangladesh’s most notable achievements is the reduction in child stunting over the past 2 decades.
The proportion of children under 5 affected by stunting fell from 54.9% in 2000 to 24% in the latest assessment, a decline of 30.9 percentage points.
However, the continued prevalence of wasting among nearly 13% of children under 5 highlights the need to address both chronic and acute malnutrition.
Stunting reflects long-term nutritional deprivation and can affect physical growth, cognitive development and educational outcomes. Wasting, meanwhile, is associated with inadequate nutrition and illness and can increase the risk of death among young children.
Public health experts say improvements in food availability alone are not enough to eliminate malnutrition. Dietary diversity, maternal nutrition, access to safe water and sanitation, health care services and household purchasing power also play crucial roles.
Speaking to Dhaka Tribune, Dr Mehbuba Nur Protha, district technical coordinator at FIVDB, said: “Although Bangladesh has made significant progress in reducing child stunting, the high prevalence of child wasting remains a serious concern, which underscores the need to strengthen maternal and child health and nutrition services at primary health care centers, ensure access to affordable, diverse diets, and improve access to safe water, sanitation, and health care, particularly for vulnerable and marginalized communities.”
The findings come amid wider concerns over the impact of economic pressures, climate-related disasters and disruptions to food systems on household food security.
For low-income families, rising food prices can make it difficult to maintain a balanced diet, even when staple foods remain available. Households may prioritize rice and other inexpensive staples over protein-rich foods, fruits, vegetables and other nutrient-dense items.
Nutrition specialists say children, pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers are particularly vulnerable when households cannot afford diverse and nutritious diets.
Dr Khondaker Golam Moazzem, research director of the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), said: “Rising food prices and stagnant household purchasing power can force low-income families to compromise on dietary diversity, making nutritious food increasingly unaffordable and worsening the risk of child malnutrition.”
Climate change is another concern, particularly for communities exposed to floods, cyclones, river erosion and salinity intrusion. Such hazards can damage crops, disrupt food supply chains, reduce household incomes and undermine access to safe drinking water.
Experts working on climate resilience and food security could help assess how these risks affect nutrition among children and vulnerable communities.
The 2026 report warns that global hunger is rising again, with conflict, climate shocks and economic crises threatening food security.
The GHI uses 4 indicators to assess hunger: undernourishment, child stunting, child wasting and under-5 mortality. Together, they capture both the availability of adequate food and the nutritional and health outcomes associated with hunger.
The index is published annually by Concern Worldwide and Welthungerhilfe, with research support from the Institute for International Law of Peace and Armed Conflict (IFHV).
Under the index’s classification system, scores below 10 indicate low hunger; scores from 10 to 19.9 indicate moderate hunger; scores from 20 to 34.9 indicate serious hunger; scores from 35 to 49.9 indicate alarming hunger; and scores of 50 or above indicate extremely alarming hunger.
Bangladesh’s score of 19.2 places it near the upper end of the moderate category, underscoring the need for sustained action to improve nutrition outcomes.
Nutrition experts say Bangladesh needs stronger coordination between food security, public health, social protection, agriculture and climate adaptation programs to make further progress.
Measures could include expanding nutrition services for mothers and young children, improving access to affordable protein-rich foods, strengthening school and community nutrition programs, and supporting climate-resilient agriculture.
Better targeting of social safety-net programs and improved monitoring of child growth could also help identify vulnerable households and direct assistance where it is most needed.
While the reduction in stunting represents substantial progress, the latest figures indicate that Bangladesh still faces significant challenges in ensuring that all children receive adequate and nutritious food.
The country’s performance in future assessments will depend not only on food availability but also on whether vulnerable households can afford diverse diets and access the health care, sanitation and social support necessary for healthy growth.

item.title: Saudi Arabia accuses Iran of encouraging Houthis in latest escalation
item.description:
A Saudi foreign ministry official on Thursday accused Iran of encouraging the Houthis in the latest escalation of their fight with the kingdom, adding that the Islamic Republic continues to arm and train the group.
“Iran continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of UN Security Council resolutions,” Dr Rayed Krimly, deputy minister for public diplomacy at the foreign ministry, said during a virtual briefing with reporters.
“We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran,” he later said.
The official said the kingdom however remained in communication with Iran, even if Tehran appeared unwilling to offer concessions.
“We continue to have direct communications with Iran,” Krimly told reporters.
“Overall, it doesn’t seem yet that the Iranians are able to provide the necessary concessions for a solution.”
The official went on to accuse the Houthis of refusing to meet in Oman in recent weeks as fighting ramped up between the two sides.
“At the beginning of this escalation, we asked them to meet in Muscat, Oman and they refused,” he added.
“This was the last communication which happened a few weeks ago.”
The world’s top crude oil exporter has in recent days come under sustained attack, including a strike on Riyadh’s international airport that was the deadliest in years, as the war with the Houthis dramatically escalates.
Yemen’s civil war reignited in July after a UN-brokered truce collapsed, months into a wider Middle East war that has rocked the region and roiled energy supplies and markets.
The conflict in the country has caused what the United Nations calls one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, leaving most of the nation’s population dependent on aid.
The Saudi-led coalition has fought the Houthis since 2015 after they seized Yemen’s capital Sanaa and forced out the internationally recognized government from the city, until a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022.

item.title: Puja Udjapan Parishad reports 34 attacks ahead of Durga Puja
item.description:
At least 34 incidents of idol vandalism, temple attacks and other related violence have been reported at Durga Puja venues across Bangladesh ahead of the Hindu community’s biggest religious festival, the Bangladesh Puja Udjapan Parishad and the Mahanagar Sarbojanin Puja Committee have said.
The two organisations called for effective measures to prevent further attacks and ensure the security of religious and ethnic minorities throughout the year.
The allegations were raised at a press conference organised by the two bodies at the Dhakeshwari National Temple complex in Dhaka on Thursday morning ahead of Sharadiya Durga Puja.
The leaders expressed hope that the festival would be celebrated peacefully and without disruption, stressing that religious festivals should unite people from all communities and reflect Bangladesh’s longstanding tradition of communal harmony.
They said they envisioned a society where Eid, Durga Puja, Christmas, Buddha Purnima and other religious and social festivals could be celebrated in a secular environment without fear or the need for police protection.
A written statement was presented at the meeting by Shubhashish Kumar Biswas (Sadhan), general secretary of the Mahanagar Sarbojanin Puja Committee.
Bangladesh Puja Udjapan Parishad General Secretary Santosh Sharma said most cases filed over attacks in the previous year had resulted in punishment, with legal proceedings initiated and charge sheets submitted.
“This year, the notable development is that a total of 34 incidents involving idol vandalism, attacks on temples and other related incidents have been reported so far,” he said.
Sharma acknowledged that negligence by some Puja committees had contributed to a few incidents. Citing an incident in Netrokona, he said security arrangements had been maintained throughout the night, but no one was on guard at dawn when the incident occurred at around 5:00am.
He also said the temple's CCTV camera was defective and therefore failed to provide surveillance.
Despite these shortcomings, the local administration had taken appropriate measures, he said, adding that arrests had been made in 11 of the 34 incidents and action had been taken in the others. Some incidents were relatively minor, he added. “We are satisfied so far,” Sharma said.
However, he stressed the need for justice for major attacks against the Hindu community over Bangladesh’s 55-year history, citing the Ramu violence, the Nasirnagar attacks, the 2021 Comilla incident and the attacks in Sunamganj.
“Even today, we are demanding justice for all these incidents and exemplary punishment for those responsible,” he said.
Among those present were Bangladesh Puja Udjapan Parishad President Basudeb Dhar, General Secretary Santosh Sharma, former presidents Advocate Subrata Chowdhury and Kajal Debnath, former general secretary Dr Chandranath Poddar, adviser Bires Chandra Saha, and Mahanagar Sarbojanin Puja Committee President Gopal Chandra Debnath, along with other leaders.
According to the written statement, incidents of idol vandalism and attacks on temples have been reported in several districts, including Sylhet, Rajbari, Panchagarh, Netrokona and Tangail, during preparations for the festival.
The statement also cited a theft at a historic Kali temple in Faridpur and attacks and looting targeting homes, shops and temples belonging to members of the Hindu community in Sunamganj.
It further reported a robbery in Naogaon involving individuals posing as intelligence agency personnel.
The organisations acknowledged that law enforcement agencies had acted promptly in several cases and arrested a number of suspects. However, they stressed that lasting protection for minorities could not depend solely on police intervention.
They called for a broader commitment to secular values and stronger social resistance to communal violence.
“Security for five days of Puja is not enough; security must be ensured for 365 days a year,” the leaders said, emphasising that building a discrimination-free Bangladesh required promoting secular values and ensuring justice for perpetrators of violence.
The written statement said the administration had assured organisers of full cooperation in holding Durga Puja celebrations nationwide. Authorities had promised adequate security, while relevant public service agencies had pledged support and assured organisers that any problems would be addressed promptly.
The Bangladesh Puja Udjapan Parishad has also issued 22-point guidelines to its district- and upazila-level units to ensure the smooth organisation of the festival.
At the meeting, the organisations reiterated their eight-point demands to protect the rights and existence of religious and ethnic minorities in Bangladesh.
The demands include enacting a minority protection law, establishing a national minority commission and forming a dedicated ministry for minority affairs. They also called for proper implementation of the Vested Property Return Act.
The organisations urged the authorities to remove bureaucratic obstacles to the return of vested properties and restore ownership and possession of land to affected individuals within the stipulated timeframe, in accordance with tribunal verdicts.
They also demanded representation of minorities in the government, parliament and all representative bodies in proportion to their share of the population.
Other demands include enacting a law to protect debottor properties, or assets dedicated to religious institutions; passing an anti-discrimination law; and transforming the Hindu Religious Welfare Trust into a foundation.
The organisations further urged the government to issue a gazette notification declaring the three days from Ashtami to Dashami during Durga Puja as public holidays.
According to the written statement, draft bills on protecting debottor properties and eliminating discrimination had already been finalised.

item.title: Durga Puja: BGB setting up 18 base camps for security at bordering puja mandaps
item.description:
Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) is setting up 18 base camps and strengthening patrols to ensure security at around 1,800 puja mandaps located within eight kilometres of the country's borders during Durga Puja.
BGB Director General Major General Mohammad Ashrafuzzaman Siddiqui disclosed the plan while talking to reporters after inspecting the security arrangements at the Ramna Kali Mandir in the capital on Thursday afternoon.
He said BGB personnel have already visited the mandaps and contacted puja committees in their respective areas to coordinate security measures.
“Risks of different kinds can arise at any time. We are collecting intelligence, receiving information from various agencies and working to ensure comprehensive security so that the celebrations can take place without disruption,” the BGB chief said.
He said the force will also ensure security at puja mandaps located within a few kilometres of its headquarters in Pilkhana and other battalion, sector and regional headquarters outside border areas, in coordination with police and other law enforcement agencies.
Ashrafuzzaman said the BGB regularly coordinates with the authorities of the Ramna Kali Mandir, Dhakeshwari National Temple and other nearby puja mandaps in the capital.
He said a 24/7 control room has been opened at BGB headquarters to maintain communication with puja mandaps.
The BGB director general added that the “Sharadiya Surokkha App”, developed under the Ministry of Home Affairs, will allow puja committee members and Ansar personnel deployed at the mandaps to contact law enforcement agencies in case of any problem or emergency.
The BGB will take prompt measures as necessary to maintain security and ensure peaceful and festive celebrations, he said.
Ashrafuzzaman also said intelligence gathering, risk assessment and security measures have been strengthened in coordination with intelligence agencies.
During the visit, he exchanged views with the president and other members of the Ramna Kali Mandir Sarbojonin Puja Udjapan Committee and conveyed his greetings to members of the Hindu community on the occasion of Durga Puja.
Other senior BGB officials were present during the inspection.

item.title: Four held over smuggling of cancer drugs abroad
item.description:
The Special Response Battalion (SRB-3) has arrested four people, including a Chinese national, for allegedly smuggling Bangladeshi medicines used to treat cancer and other serious diseases abroad.
The arrestees are Chinese national Li Fen, 34; Bakul Nahar Bithi, 24, from Rangpur; Yunus Ali, 26, from Satkhira; and Sajib Howlader, 28, from Patuakhali.
The elite force also seized medicines worth around Tk7.5 crore and Tk6,06,140 in cash from the alleged smuggling ring.
SRB-3 Commander Lt Col Faizul Arefin disclosed the details at a press briefing at the force’s headquarters in Shahjahanpur, Dhaka, on Thursday afternoon.
He said the four were arrested during a raid in Uttara on Wednesday evening for allegedly smuggling medicines abroad and evading government revenue.
According to SRB-3, Li Fen entered Bangladesh in August 2024 on a 30-day tourist visa. Two to three days before his visa expired, he would return to China and then re-enter Bangladesh on another tourist visa within a day or two.
Bithi studied business administration at Hunan Normal University in China from 2019 to 2023 and learned Chinese language there. After returning to Bangladesh, she worked as an interpreter for Chinese nationals.
The gang allegedly bought medicines at relatively low prices in Bangladesh and shipped them abroad for higher profits. The medicines were sent by courier to countries including Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam.
The consignments included drugs used to treat cancer and other complex and chronic diseases, SRB-3 said.
Investigators found that the gang packed 24-25kg of medicines in each carton for shipment abroad.
Lt Col Arefin said Laos customs authorities seized a 100kg consignment of medicines on October 13 after it was sent by courier without valid documentation.
He said the illegal export of medicines without following relevant laws and regulations had tarnished Bangladesh’s image internationally.
The preliminary investigation also found evidence of links between the gang and some unscrupulous employees of pharmaceutical companies, who allegedly became involved in the illegal trade of medicines for higher profits.

Once operational, the expressway is expected to improve connectivity between Munshiganj, Narayanganj, and surrounding areas, making travel safer and more convenient.

item.title: 18.1 million in Bangladesh at risk of food insecurity: WFP
item.description:
The number of people in Bangladesh at risk of food insecurity has increased. According to a report by the World Food Programme (WFP), the number of people facing acute food insecurity could reach 18.1 million between September and December this year, up by 2.8 million from the beginning of the year.

The WFP report was published on 22 September. It highlighted concerns over inflation, declining purchasing power, agricultural losses caused by floods, child malnutrition and uncertainty over food assistance for Rohingya refugees.

Today, 16 October, is World Food Day. The decision to observe the day was taken at the 20th session of the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) in 1979. The first World Food Day was observed in 1981. This year’s theme is “Innovate today, nourish tomorrow.”

The day is being observed at a time when Bangladesh has been grappling with high inflation for a long time. Economic growth has slowed, while employment opportunities remain limited.

Several surveys have also indicated that poverty has increased in the country. Analysts say a section of the population has always faced food insecurity and the WFP report shows that the number of people at risk has grown further.

According to the WFP report, food shortages and malnutrition are hampering children’s growth. Inadequate food intake and a lack of essential nutrients pose risks to their normal growth and development.

In Bangladesh, one in four children under five is stunted, while 11 per cent are wasted. Two out of every five households also face significant micronutrient deficiencies.

The report further says floods and waterlogging damaged around 80,000 hectares of agricultural land in Bangladesh in 2026. The damage affected 230,000 farming households and 1.3 million people, disrupting food production and livelihoods.

The report also pointed to global and regional risks affecting the country’s food security. Nearly half of Bangladesh’s remittance inflows come from the Middle East but there are concerns that the flow of remittances could be disrupted.

High Inflation

Food prices in Bangladesh began rising after the Russia-Ukraine war broke out in early 2022. Food inflation exceeded 14 per cent in July 2024, the highest level in more than a decade. It remained above 10 per cent for several months before falling below that level recently.

According to data released by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) in September, food inflation stood at 7.22 per cent that month, while non-food inflation was 9.3 per cent.

A decline in food inflation does not mean that prices have fallen. It means only that the rate at which prices are rising has slowed slightly.

In a forecast on 13 October, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said Bangladesh’s gross domestic product (GDP) growth could fall to 3.2 per cent in the current 2026–27 fiscal year. Average inflation could rise to 10.9 per cent over the same period.

The projections have raised concerns over economic recovery, people’s purchasing power and the investment climate.

According to the state-run Trading Corporation of Bangladesh (TCB), coarse rice is currently selling for at least Tk 50 per kilogram in the market. Loose ata is also selling at the same price.

Data from the Ministry of Food show that 834,000 tonnes of rice and wheat were distributed under various programmes between 1 July and 8 October, 48,000 tonnes less than during the same period last year. However, foodgrain stocks stand at around 2.35 million tonnes, which is considered a reasonably healthy level.

Selim Raihan, professor of economics at the University of Dhaka and executive director of the South Asian Network on Economic Modeling (SANEM), told Prothom Alo that the government’s first priority in addressing the current risk of food insecurity should be to identify the most vulnerable groups and ensure they receive timely and effective assistance.

According to him, the government should expand food assistance, sales of rice, lentils and other essential commodities at fair prices, and targeted cash support for low-income households, day labourers, agricultural workers, female-headed households and people living in disaster-affected areas.

Selim Raihan also said regular monitoring was essential to prevent artificial shortages, hoarding and market manipulation, while ensuring transparency in the supply chain.

Report: Data of 1.8 million Bangladesh users found on dark web
item.description:
Data belonging to more than 1.8 million users in Bangladesh, along with at least 17,362 sets of login credentials, have been found on the dark web, according to a report by CyberStation, the cybersecurity division of Brain Station 23 PLC.
The findings were presented at an event titled “Bangladesh Cyber Resilience Briefing 2026” held at Brac Centre on Thursday.
Around 150 representatives from the government, banking, telecommunications, technology and education sectors attended the event, along with representatives of regulatory bodies and cybersecurity experts.
According to a press release, CyberStation reviewed 767 domains across 15 sectors and found evidence of personal data exposure in almost all of them.
The report found that the government services sector accounted for the largest share of exposed citizens’ data, while the technology and telecommunications sectors had the highest rates of data exposure.
CyberStation said the figures were minimum estimates and that the actual numbers could be higher.
Speaking at the event, Mohibbullah Moktadir Tanim, head of cybersecurity services at CyberStation, said: “We cannot mitigate risks that we cannot see.”
He said identifying what data had been exposed would allow the necessary steps to be taken before criminals could misuse it.
Brain Station 23 Executive Director M J Ferdous stressed the need to reduce reliance on foreign software to strengthen the country’s cybersecurity infrastructure.
Cybersecurity analyst Tanvir Hasan Zoha, meanwhile, emphasised the importance of raising public awareness and developing effective preventive strategies.
A panel discussion at the event focused on the risks of data exposure on the dark web and ways to address them. Participants highlighted the need for coordinated efforts among relevant stakeholders to prevent the misuse of personal information.

item.title: BRTA makes front number plates mandatory for motorcycles
item.description:
The Bangladesh Road Transport Authority (BRTA) has made it mandatory for motorcycles to display number plates at the front, setting November 15 as the deadline for installation.
Motorcycle owners must install manually made number plates at the front in addition to the digital plates already required at the rear. Those who fail to comply by the deadline will face legal action, it said.
In an urgent public notice issued on Friday, the BRTA said the Road Transport Act, 2018 and the Road Transport Rules, 2022 already require motorcycles to have retro-reflective number plates equipped with Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) tags at the rear.
To strengthen traffic management and surveillance, the authority has now decided to require registration numbers to be displayed at the front as well.
The front number plates must be made of stainless steel or aluminium, with a white background and black Bengali letters and numerals. No designs or decorative elements will be allowed.
The notice also specifies different dimensions for scooters and other motorcycles.
For scooters, the plate must be 200mm long and 100mm wide, while for other motorcycles, it must be 285mm long and 50mm wide. In both cases, the letters and numerals must be at least 20mm high.
The BRTA has urged motorcycle owners to install the plates in accordance with the prescribed specifications before the deadline.

item.title: Bangladesh unaware of execution of 2 nationals in Mecca, writes to Saudi Arabia seeking details
item.description:
Bangladesh was not informed in advance about the execution of two Bangladeshi nationals in Saudi Arabia’s holy city of Mecca for allegedly engaging in “indecent” acts in a mosque area.

Bangladesh learned of the executions after reports appeared in the media. The Bangladesh Consulate in Jeddah wrote to the Saudi foreign ministry on Thursday seeking detailed information about the incident.

Sources at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Dhaka and the Bangladesh Consulate in Jeddah confirmed the matter to Prothom Alo.

A source at the Bangladesh Consulate in Jeddah told this correspondent on Friday afternoon that Saudi authorities had not formally informed Bangladesh about the executions beforehand. The matter came to the consulate’s attention only after the news was published in the media. The consulate subsequently sent a letter to the Saudi foreign ministry on Thursday, requesting details of the incident.

The Saudi Press Agency (SPA), citing the country’s interior ministry, confirmed the executions on Wednesday. The two people executed have been identified as Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akhtar.

Middle Eastern news outlet Gulf News reported that Saudi security forces had arrested them on allegations of engaging in immoral and indecent acts at a mosque in Mecca.

According to the report, after their arrest and an initial investigation, specific charges were brought against the two and the case was referred to court. Under Sharia law, the court sentenced them to death under ta'zir, a category of discretionary punishment determined by a judge.

The report said the judge imposed the sentence after considering the desecration of the mosque’s sanctity and the circumstances in which the alleged offence took place. The verdict was subsequently upheld by higher judicial authorities, making it final, and a royal order was issued for the executions.

In a statement, Saudi Arabia’s interior ministry reiterated the government’s firm position on protecting the security of the holy mosques, upholding justice and enforcing Sharia law against those who violate religious sanctity. It also warned that anyone committing similar offences at holy sites would face severe punishment.

Private sources in Saudi Arabia said the judicial proceedings had been under way at a court in Jeddah for several months. Two prominent Bangladeshi citizens reportedly assisted as interpreters during the proceedings.

Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia are both parties to the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations. Article 36 of the convention stipulates that when a foreign national is arrested, the detaining country must, at the detainee’s request, notify the person’s consulate without delay and allow access to consular assistance. It remains unclear whether the two detainees had requested that the Bangladeshi consulate be notified.

Several officials at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Saudi authorities would not ordinarily arrest two Bangladeshi nationals and execute them so quickly. They also described it as puzzling that no one acting on behalf of the two had contacted the Bangladeshi mission.

No information has yet emerged about the two individuals’ immigration status or length of stay in Saudi Arabia, or whether they received legal assistance or had the opportunity to appeal during the proceedings.

item.title: Muhammad Yunus receives ‘Hillary Rodham Clinton Award’
item.description:
Former chief adviser to the interim government of Bangladesh and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Muhammad Yunus has received the prestigious ‘Hillary Rodham Clinton Award’.

Former US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton presented the award to Grameen Bank founder Muhammad Yunus at a grand ceremony held at Georgetown University in Washington on Thursday.

Around 400 guests, including ambassadors from about 25 countries, entrepreneurs, teachers and researchers, attended the ceremony at the university’s Gaston Hall.

As soon as Muhammad Yunus’s name was announced, the audience rose to its feet and gave him a prolonged standing ovation.

A total of four people, including Muhammad Yunus, received the honour this year. The other recipients were India’s Self-Employed Women’s Association (SEWA) director Reema Nanavaty, Tory Burch Foundation founder and fashion designer Tory Burch and board chair of Jordan’s Microfund for Women Muna Sukhtian.

Muna also received the special ‘Georgetown Ambassadors Award’.

Praising Muhammad Yunus at the ceremony, Hillary Clinton said, “I have personally seen the work of Grameen Bank and seen how women have become self-reliant and ensured their own security and empowerment.”

Describing the work as unprecedented, she said, “It is not only the women of Bangladesh but Dr Yunus has spread his work across the world.”

In his acceptance speech, Muhammad Yunus referred to the completion of 50 years of his work and said, “This is a recognition of 50 years of our work. The event you have organised here will convey an important message to Bangladesh and inspire Grameen families.”

Highlighting Grameen Bank’s role in poverty alleviation and women’s empowerment, he said, “Through microcredit, we have helped people living in extreme poverty stand on their own feet.”

“We have focused on women so that they can use their own strengths, take responsibility for themselves and improve their families’ financial conditions,” he added.

“Today, we no longer see poor women sitting quietly and shyly. Instead, we see confident women who speak up about their problems and needs. These women run their own bank, and they are the owners of Grameen Bank,” Yunus added.

Referring to the children of borrowers who are now seeking employment, Yunus said they had been told to repeat the message, “We are not job seekers, we are job creators.”

Speaking about the concept of social business, he said its purpose was not to generate personal profit but to solve problems.

“Social business funds are supporting the establishment of hospitals, healthcare centres and eye hospitals in different parts of the country. Any surplus generated by these institutions is being reinvested in healthcare,” he added.

Criticising the current education system, Muhammad Yunus said it had been wrongly structured because it prepared young people to seek jobs.

“The purpose of education should be to develop people’s creativity and entrepreneurial spirit and the education system should focus on creating entrepreneurs,”

Muhammad Yunus also revealed that Grameen University would be launched by the end of this year to help achieve that goal, according to a press release.

He said Grameen University could take the lead in building a “Three Zeros” world.

“The university will seek to teach students to become entrepreneurs instead of merely pursuing certificates. It will provide the necessary support, including financing, to help them start businesses,” he added.

He hoped that the initiative would mark a new beginning in the field of education.

item.title: Question paper reaches 2 NBR employees before dawn, spreads with answers within hours
item.description:
At 4:43 am, a blurry photograph of the question paper arrived on the mobile phone of Nur Mohammad, an office assistant at the National Board of Revenue (NBR). Nearly an hour and a half later, at around 6:15 am, Jahangir, a computer operator at the same organisation, received a clearer photograph of the same question paper.

An answer sheet was then prepared and circulated among other members of the network. Through them, it reached prospective candidates and people seeking to buy the leaked questions.

The Special Response Battalion (SRB) said it had pieced together this sequence by examining mobile phone conversations and data retrieved from the phones of those arrested in connection with the leak of the recruitment examination questions for assistant youth development officer posts at the Department of Youth Development.

Over the past three days, the force arrested seven people in raids in Dhaka and elsewhere in the country. Besides NBR employees, those arrested include staff members of the Department of Environment and the Ministry of Defence.

Based on information provided by the arrestees, the force seized 116 stamp papers each costs Tk 100, four Tk 50 stamp papers, a set of question papers, 19 pages of admission cards for various examinations, 10 certificates of different categories, another 15 certificates of various types, 48 pages of bank cheques from different banks, a cheque book from one bank, six national identity cards and Tk 4,000 in cash.

The arrestees are Nur Mohammad, 30, an office assistant at the NBR; Jahangir, 38, an NBR computer operator; SM Imdadul Islam, 35, an NBR computer operator; Asadul Islam, 33, an office assistant at the Ministry of Defence; Md Rubel Islam, 33, a data entry operator at the Department of Environment; and two other members of the network, Mofizul Islam, 23, and Md Hasinur Rahman alias Sujon.

Lieutenant Colonel Faizul Arefin, commander of SRB-3, disclosed the information at a press conference at the SRB media centre in Karwan Bazar, Dhaka, on Friday afternoon.

Last Saturday, candidates took to the streets and blocked roads in different parts of Dhaka to protest the question paper leak in the Department of Youth Development recruitment examination.

The Ministry of Youth and Sports formed a five-member committee the same day to investigate the allegations, appointing an additional secretary to head it. The committee has yet to submit its report. Meanwhile, the recruitment examination was held again today.

Shadow investigation launched after question paper leak

Lieutenant Colonel Faizul Arefin, commander of SRB-3, said the recruitment test for 242 vacant assistant youth development officer posts at the Department of Youth Development had been scheduled for 10 October. A total of 319,000 jobseekers had applied.

The examination was scheduled to begin at 11:00 am that day, but the authorities postponed it after confirming the question paper leak at 10:03 am.

The SRB launched a shadow investigation following the incident. On 11 October, the Department of Youth Development filed a case with Motijheel police station. The SRB intelligence team began investigating to identify the possible source of the question paper, those supplying it, intermediaries distributing it and its buyers.

The force subsequently found evidence pointing to the involvement of an organised network. Acting on that information, it arrested seven people in raids in Dhaka and elsewhere on 14, 15 and 16 October.

Raids began in Motijheel before spreading to other areas

At the press conference, the SRB said preliminary inquiries had pointed to the involvement of Rubel Islam, a data entry operator at the Department of Environment. He was arrested along with two others in Motijheel, Dhaka, while money was allegedly being transferred in connection with an admission-related racket.

Mofizul, one of those arrested, is a jobseeker. After being defrauded of Tk 1.7 million by a member of a racket, he joined the network in the hope of making more money.

Information provided by the arrestees and an analysis of their mobile phone conversations led investigators to other members of the network. SM Imdadul Islam, a computer operator at the NBR, was arrested in the Uttarkhan area, while Asadul Islam, an office assistant at the Ministry of Defence, was arrested in Mirpur-10, Dhaka.

Later, based on mobile phone chat records, SRB-4 arrested NBR office assistant Nur Mohammad in Savar on Thursday. On Friday, evidence and information obtained from him led to the arrest of Jahangir, a computer operator at the same organisation, in Mohammadpur.

From question paper to answer sheet, then distribution

Lieutenant Colonel Faizul Arefin said an examination of messages exchanged on the arrested individuals’ mobile phones had revealed a sequence of events showing how the question paper was obtained and distributed.

According to the investigation, at around 4:43 am on 10 October, NBR office assistant Nur Mohammad received a blurry photograph of the question paper from an unidentified source. At around 6:15 am, Jahangir sent him a clearer photograph of the paper.

Nur Mohammad then prepared answers to the questions and sent them to Jahangir and his colleague Imdadul Islam. Preliminary findings suggest that the information was subsequently passed on to the network members’ own candidates and those involved in distributing the leaked questions.

Investigators found indications of the involvement of Asadul Islam, Rubel Islam, Mofizul Islam and Hasinur Rahman Sujon.

The network used fake identities on WhatsApp to communicate and conduct transactions. Its members sold the leaked questions and answer sheets to candidates they knew for Tk 800,000 to Tk 1 million.

During questioning, the suspects did not disclose how many people had bought the questions from them. They said they had been involved in leaking question papers for various recruitment examinations.

According to their statements, they charged Tk 800,000 to Tk 1 million for question papers for third-class recruitment examinations and Tk 1.5 million to Tk 2 million for second-class recruitment examinations.

During questioning, Nur Mohammad and Jahangir failed to give satisfactory answers about who had supplied them with the question paper for the assistant youth development officer recruitment examination.

Asked whether anyone at the Department of Youth Development had been involved in the leak, SRB official Faizul Arefin said the matter could be confirmed after the investigation was completed.
