item.title: TIB: State reform held hostage by power politics a year after July Charter signing
item.description:
Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB) has said the opportunity to establish an accountable system of government and reform the state created by the July mass uprising has been held hostage by power politics and a bureaucratic vicious cycle, a year after the July National Charter was signed.
TIB Executive Director Iftekharuzzaman made the remarks in a statement on Friday, expressing concern over the direction of state reforms and the government’s decisions on constitutional changes, judicial independence and accountability.
According to Iftekharuzzaman, the interim government failed to make the most of the opportunity created by the July mass uprising because of a lack of strategic planning and political courage, alongside compromises with bureaucratic resistance.
Following the 13th parliamentary election, the legal, institutional and bureaucratic ecosystem has continued to be shaped by power politics, he said. The reform process has therefore remained constrained by political interests rather than being directed towards establishing an accountable system of government.
The decisions taken by the government have raised questions about its commitment to the reform agenda, particularly where changes depend on political consensus and the willingness of those in power to accept greater accountability.
The ruling alliance’s position on constitutional amendments and state reform, alongside opposition parties’ pursuit of partisan gains, has complicated the implementation of the reform agenda.
The ruling party had presented a 31-point agenda and pledged in its election manifesto to implement state reforms and the July National Charter “to the letter”.
However, ruling party members of parliament refused to take the oath as members of the proposed Constitutional Reform Council despite having supported the referendum, raising questions about the implementation of the reform commitments.
The role of the Constitutional Amendment Committee has also become part of the wider debate over the future of the reform process and the extent to which political parties are prepared to honour their commitments.
The interim government issued 133 ordinances, many of which the current government has since enacted. However, decisions to repeal or suspend accountability-related ordinances while enacting measures that make executive powers less accountable have raised concerns about the direction of reform.
The slogan “Now it is our turn” has also drawn attention in the context of questions about whether the political transition is delivering institutional change or reproducing existing patterns of power.
Among the measures repealed were the Supreme Court Secretariat (Amendment) Ordinance and the Supreme Court Judges Appointment Ordinance.
Instead of proceeding with the amended bill concerning the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC), the government returned to the ACC Act 2004.
The National Human Rights Commission Ordinance was also repealed and replaced with a new law. The ordinance on enforced disappearances was repealed, while legislation was introduced that, according to the criticism raised over the changes, protects the agencies concerned.
Although the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB) was said to have been abolished, the force was further empowered under a new name.
The absence of an independent police commission has also raised concerns about accountability in law enforcement. Similarly, there has been no clear indication that asset declarations required within three months of taking office are being implemented.
The decisions affecting the judiciary, law enforcement agencies, the ACC and the National Human Rights Commission have raised broader concerns about the independence of institutions responsible for ensuring accountability.
Iftekharuzzaman’s concerns centre on the risk that institutions meant to provide oversight could become partisan, weakening their ability to hold the executive branch accountable.
The developments have also raised questions about whether the reform process is addressing the institutional weaknesses associated with authoritarian rule or allowing similar patterns to persist under a new political arrangement.
The concerns extend beyond individual ordinances or institutions to the wider system of checks and balances, including the independence of the judiciary and the effectiveness of mechanisms designed to investigate abuses and prevent the misuse of state power.
TIB has called on political parties to uphold the consensus reached on the July National Charter and follow through on their commitments to state reform.
The organisation has stressed the importance of implementing the agreed reforms to strengthen democracy, improve governance and ensure social justice.
It has also warned against allowing partisan interests and bureaucratic resistance to undermine the opportunity for meaningful institutional change created by the July mass uprising.
TIB’s call comes amid concerns that failure to honour the reform commitments could leave the country vulnerable to a return to authoritarian rule.

item.title: 107 flights to Saudi Arabia cancelled, 16,620 passengers stranded
item.description:
A total of 107 flights from Dhaka to Riyadh and Dammam airports were cancelled from October 10 to Friday due to the closure of the 2 airports, leaving 16,620 passengers stranded.
Kawser Mahmud, assistant director of the public relations department of the Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB), confirmed the information on Friday afternoon.
He said 44 of the cancelled flights were direct flights, including 17 operated by Biman Bangladesh Airlines, 10 by US-Bangla Airlines, 10 by Saudia and 7 by Riyadh Air.
Another 63 transit flights were cancelled. These included 22 operated by IndiGo, 7 by SalamAir, 1 by EgyptAir, 14 by Emirates, 9 by Qatar Airways, 6 by flydubai and 4 by Air India.
Mahmud said flight cancellations would continue until the situation returned to normal and the airports resumed normal operations.

item.title: Dengue: Four more die, 1,181 hospitalized in 24 hours
item.description:
Four people died of dengue, and 1,181 were hospitalized after being infected with dengue in the last 24 hours till 8am on Friday, according to a regular report of Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
With four deaths in the past 24 hours, the death toll from the disease stood at 335 this year.
Of the newly hospitalized dengue patients, 410 were in Dhaka Division, 92 in Mymensingh Division, 242 in Chittagong Division, 140 in Khulna Division, 99 in Rajshahi, 71 in Rangpur Division and 127 in Barisal Division.
According to the report, a total of 108,440 dengue patients have so far been hospitalized across the country this year.
However, in the last 24 hours, 1,179 patients recovered and were discharged from hospitals.
So far, 102,210 dengue patients have recovered and returned home after receiving treatment in hospitals.
A total of 102,861 people were infected with dengue, and 413 people died from the disease last year.

item.title: Titumir: WB, IMF see Family, Farmers’ Card helping reduce poverty
item.description:
The World Bank (WB) and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) believe the government's Family Card, Farmers' Card and other social protection programs can help ease people's economic hardship and reduce poverty amid prolonged inflation and the ongoing Middle East crisis.
The initiatives are expected to help lift people who have fallen below the poverty line out of poverty while preventing vulnerable households from slipping into poverty, said Prime Minister's Adviser on Finance and Planning Prof Dr Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir.
He made the remarks on Friday while briefing journalists on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group in Bangkok.
Earlier in the morning, a Bangladesh delegation led by Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury held meetings with officials of the World Bank, IMF, Standard Chartered Bank and Bank of America.
Dr Titumir said prolonged inflation and the Middle East crisis had increased the cost of living, particularly for low-income and working-class people.
Rising fuel and electricity prices could also affect various sectors of the economy, he added.
"The government is taking necessary measures to address these pressures," he said, adding that it is trying to minimize the additional burden on ordinary people when adjusting fuel prices.
Referring to recent World Bank reports and assessments by international organizations, the adviser said prolonged inflation had increased the risk of more people falling below the poverty line.
According to World Bank estimates cited by him, around eight million people in Bangladesh had fallen below the poverty line due to prolonged inflation in the past.
He said the Family Card and Farmers' Card programs were expected to play an important role in addressing the situation.
One of the major weaknesses of previous social safety net programs was the inaccurate selection of beneficiaries, Dr Titumir said.
Many eligible people were excluded, while some ineligible individuals were included in the lists, he added.
To address the problem, the government is emphasizing the use of digital public infrastructure to ensure that assistance reaches the actual beneficiaries, he said.
Citing assessments by independent research organizations, the adviser said effective implementation of the Family Card program could reduce poverty by around 5%.
He said the programs were not merely aspirational plans but were included in the Prime Minister's election manifesto and the government's five-year economic strategy.
Dr Titumir said strict monetary policy alone would not be sufficient to control inflation, stressing the need for reforms in revenue collection and the financial sector.
The government aims to increase revenue mobilization and move away from tax evasion, tax fraud and a culture of patronage, he said, adding that revenue collection had already shown positive changes following the reform initiatives.
Revenue growth stood at around 3% in the last fiscal year. However, after the present government assumed office, revenue growth rose to 12-13% during the period from mid-February to June 30, he said.
The credibility of the government's reform agenda would be demonstrated through tangible results, the adviser added.
Regarding the IMF's economic projections, he said forecasts should be interpreted in light of their underlying assumptions and the prevailing circumstances.
"The projections should also be viewed against the possible consequences of failing to implement reforms," he said, adding that the government wanted to overcome doubts among international partners stemming from unfulfilled commitments under the previous Sheikh Hasina administration.
Highlighting the need to restore discipline in the banking sector and rebuild depositors' confidence, Dr Titumir said financial losses equivalent to around US$40 billion had come to the fore following widespread irregularities and the siphoning of funds in the past.
The government was working to restore confidence in the banking system, he said.
He noted progress in rebuilding depositors' confidence in Sammilito Islami Bank, saying customers had been able to withdraw money according to their needs since September 1.
Many depositors were also placing money in the bank while withdrawing funds, which he described as an indication of improving confidence.
The decline in Treasury bond interest rates was another positive sign of changes in the financial sector, he added.
Dr Titumir said the Middle East crisis had increased import costs for fuel, liquefied natural gas (LNG) and fertilizer.
However, calculating the additional import expenditure alone would not fully capture the crisis's impact on the economy, he said.
The government's decision to refrain from increasing diesel prices to reduce pressure on farmers should also be taken into account, he added.
Although Bangladesh had no role in creating the crisis, the government was working to address its consequences out of its responsibility to the people, he said.
The adviser said the prime minister had adopted a strategy to transform Bangladesh into a manufacturing hub and an export gateway to accelerate economic recovery, create jobs and increase production and exports.
The government's objectives include boosting domestic revenue, restoring confidence in the banking sector and reducing economic pressure on households to create a pathway towards sustainable development, he added.
The 2026 Annual Meetings of the World Bank Group and the IMF are being held in Bangkok, Thailand from October 12 to 18.
The meetings at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center have brought together finance ministers, central bank governors, policymakers, development partners and private-sector representatives from across the world.
Global economic challenges, development financing, poverty reduction, job creation, investment expansion and financial-sector reforms are among the key issues under discussion.
For Bangladesh, the meetings provide an important opportunity to advance discussions with international partners on economic reforms, development financing and programs aligned with the country's priorities.

item.title: National Parliament committee proposes annual assessments to enhance education quality
item.description:
The Standing Committee on the Ministry of Education of the 13th National Parliament has recommended introducing an annual assessment system aligned with international standards to improve quality of education and move beyond artificial competition over pass rates.
At its first meeting held at the National Parliament Building on September 10, the committee proposed a series of measures to ensure transparency in education spending, tackle irregularities and corruption, investigate declining secondary-level enrolment, strengthen teacher training and expand technical education.
Chairman of the committee and Member of Parliament Md Salim Bhuiyan told Bangladesh Sangbad Sangstha (BSS) at the Secretariat yesterday that the previous government had focused on numerical indicators and pass rates rather than genuine educational quality.
“Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's government does not believe in this artificial competition. We want to ensure genuine quality in education in the country,” he said.
He stressed the need for annual assessments, a modern curriculum and evaluations of learning outcomes at three- or six-month intervals to bring students in line with international standards.
Further recommendations and details of the government's education roadmap will be presented at a press conference, he added.
Committee member Reza Kibria also emphasized setting specific annual benchmarks to ensure Bangladeshi students perform competitively in international assessments, particularly in mathematics and science.
Members proposed a long-term national education vision, modelled on Malaysia, to prevent frequent changes to education policies, curricula and textbooks following changes in government.
According to the meeting minutes, the government has proposed a budget of Tk57,301.68 crore for the Secondary and Higher Education Division in the 2026-27 fiscal year, 42.7% higher than the previous revised budget.
The initiatives discussed included distributing laptops to approximately 40,000 students who achieved a Golden GPA in 2026 and bringing seven million female students under a Tk4,000 crore scholarship program to promote girls’ education and reduce dropout rates.
The committee also acknowledged the transfer of outstanding dues to the bank accounts of around 70,000 retired teachers and employees through the Electronic Fund Transfer (EFT) and iBAS systems.
In the initial phase, each teacher is receiving an average of Tk5 lakh.
The committee thanked Prime Minister Tarique Rahman for providing Tk2,000 crore in special assistance to address the crisis involving teachers' welfare and retirement benefits.
It recommended expediting MPO enlistment for eligible non-MPO institutions and long-serving teachers, reducing bureaucratic delays and investigating the significant decline in secondary-level enrolment.
Technical and Madrasah Education Division Secretary (routine charge) Shamsur Rahman Khan informed the meeting that technical education enrolment reached 19.16% in 2025, with a target of 30% by 2030.
Other decisions included field visits by committee members to inspect educational institutions, mandatory attendance of education board heads and National University representatives at future meetings, and faster settlement of outstanding allowances, subject to budget availability.
Educationists have welcomed the proposals, particularly the shift towards measurable learning outcomes and international standards, as potentially significant steps towards improving education quality.

item.title: Speakers: Climate-vulnerable countries must not be pushed into debt trap
item.description:
Climate-vulnerable countries must not be pushed into a new debt trap in the name of climate adaptation, speakers said at a human chain program in Mongla on Friday.
They said developed countries and corporations continue to profit from fossil fuel-dependent economies, while farmers, workers and climate-vulnerable nations bear the brunt of cyclones, droughts, river erosion and crop losses.
The speakers called for a just transition to green energy, environmental protection, climate justice and public ownership of resources.
The human chain program was held at Mithekhali Bazar in Mongla, coinciding with the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank in Bangkok, Thailand, scheduled for October 12-18. The event focused on the question of whose interests the global economy serves.
Dharitri Rakkhay Amra, Pashur River Waterkeeper, Udayan Youth Sangha, and Waterkeepers Bangladesh jointly organised the program.
Nur Alam Sheikh, a central leader of DHORA and Pashur River Waterkeeper, presided over the event. Speakers included Prof Nazrul Islam, labour leader Nazmul Haque, DHORA leader Molla Al Mamun, farmer leader Asaduzzaman Tito, SM Jane Alam Babu of Udayan Youth Sangha, youth leaders Sheikh Sifatullah Shuvo and Arafat Durjoy, and Mehedi Hasan of Waterkeepers Bangladesh.
Nazmul Haque said developing countries were struggling to repay foreign loans and interest while meeting essential spending needs in education, healthcare, agriculture and social protection. High interest rates, rising energy prices and climate-related disasters were further aggravating the crisis, he said.
“If people’s fundamental rights are curtailed to repay loans, who is development for?” he asked, stressing that public needs must take precedence over lenders’ conditions.
In his address, Nur Alam Sheikh said communities affected by climate change should receive fair compensation, not loans, for the losses and damage they suffer. “We must build a world for people, not for profit,” he said, calling for adequate climate financing and investment in renewable energy.
He also urged the government to ensure that food was treated as a fundamental human right rather than a source of corporate profit, promote environmentally friendly agriculture and ensure a just transition to green energy.
“Financing renewable energy is financing climate action,” he said, calling for an immediate shift to renewable energy.

item.title: European leaders rally around Zelensky as Trump ties slump
item.description:
European leaders on Friday rallied around Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelensky as Kyiv’s ties with US President Donald Trump have nosedived and worries grow that US leader is increasingly siding with Russia.
Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured since last week, when Trump eased sanctions on Russia in exchange for Moscow releasing large amounts of diesel onto global markets.
Zelensky infuriated Trump further by ordering Ukraine’s forces to restart strikes on Russian oil refineries in defiance of Washington’s demands.
Meanwhile anger in Ukraine has been heightened by disruptions to a critical US-provided satellite system that has hampered its military’s ability to counter Russia’s intense bombardments ahead of the harsh winter months.
“This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine. This is no time to relieve Russia’s sanctions,” European Council chief Antonio Costa said, standing alongside Zelensky at an EU summit in Brussels. “Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure.”
The Ukrainian president welcomed the backing of “real leaders” in Europe and said there were no signals that Moscow is ready “to end this war.”
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said that “the situation in Ukraine is currently truly dire, with numerous Russian attacks and a tense relationship between Ukraine and the US.”
“It is crucial that we, as Europe, demonstrate our unconditional support for them today -- and explore what additional steps we can take,” he said.
Zelensky has had to endure a rollercoaster relationship with Trump since the mercurial US leader returned to office last year vowing to cut Washington’s support for Kyiv.
Trump on Thursday branded renewed Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil infrastructure a “disgrace” and said Kyiv was driving up global energy prices.
“I think I find Zelensky to be more difficult to deal with than Putin,” the US leader said in an interview with Newsmax.
The Kremlin has sought to capitalize on the latest breakdown between Kyiv and Washington, blaming Ukraine for derailing US peace efforts by resuming its strikes on refineries.
Ukraine meanwhile has accused the Trump administration of essentially helping Moscow during the latest falling out as the bad blood appears to have hit Ukraine’s ability to defend itself.
Despite the tensions, European leaders are hoping that Ukraine can weather the storm and patch up ties as there is little substitute for key US satellite capabilities.
“Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine and unfortunately in (the) short term Europe can’t replace this capability,” EU top diplomat Kaja Kallas said.
Ukraine uses the Starshield system from Elon Musk’s SpaceX for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territory and interceptor drones.
It is separate from SpaceX’s parallel Starlink civilian satellite system, which Ukraine also uses but not for offensive operations.
Tech billionaire Musk, who has also called for Zelensky to be replaced as leader, said his company was not behind any disruption to the system.
“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” he added, referring to Trump.
While the main focus for European leaders will be on overcoming the latest crisis with Washington, they will also focus on how to bolster Ukraine’s air defenses and cover Ukraine’s dire budgetary situation.
“We have to prepare for the winter. It’s not only energy, it’s also air defense and fundings,” Zelensky said.
EU leaders are set to open discussions about how to keep Ukraine afloat next year in the face of a growing realization that funds will run dry.
The EU has in place a $101-billion loan for Kyiv that was set to help cover funding to the end of 2027.
But the Ukrainian authorities have warned they will need tens of billions more as Russia’s strikes have battered the country’s economy.
The talks around the new funding have reignited calls for the European Union to tap around 200 billion euros in frozen Russian central bank assets to fund Ukraine.
“The frozen assets are there. That’s what should be used for supporting Ukraine,” said Latvian premier Andris Kulbergs.
But there seems little momentum on that front as Belgium, where most of the funds are held, remains opposed.

item.title: Eighteen passenger railway coaches arrive from India
item.description:
Eighteen broad-gauge passenger railway coaches imported from India entered Bangladesh through the Darshana-Jaynagar border in Chuadanga at 3pm on Friday.
After completing customs formalities at Darshana, the coaches will be taken to Bangladesh Railway’s workshop in Saidpur for inspection before being added to the railway fleet.
The coaches began their journey from Kapurthala in India’s Punjab state on Monday, October 12. They remained at Ranaghat Station in Kolkata before departing on Friday afternoon.
After completing formalities at India’s Gede border checkpoint, the coaches entered Bangladesh through the Darshana-Jaynagar border. Officials of Bangladesh Railway’s Pakshey division subsequently took charge of the shipment.
The coaches have been painted red and green. The shipment includes 3 air-conditioned chair coaches, air-conditioned berth coaches, 4 luggage vans and 11 Shovon chair coaches.
In May 2024, the Bangladesh government signed an agreement with India’s RITES Limited under a project to purchase broad-gauge railway coaches.
The coaches were procured from RITES Limited in India. A total of 200 coaches will be collected from India in several phases and added to Bangladesh Railway’s fleet.
Robiul Islam, divisional mechanical engineer of Bangladesh Railway’s Pakshey division, said 18 broad-gauge passenger coaches had entered Bangladesh from India on Friday.
He said the coaches belonged to different categories and that the government had taken the initiative to improve the quality of passenger services.

item.description:
A fire broke out at a wooden resort and restaurant on Patuartek Sea Beach in Inani of Ukhiya, Cox’s Bazar.

The fire started at around 7:30am today, Saturday. The district administration has confirmed four deaths in the incident.

Cox’s Bazar Deputy Commissioner Md A Mannan told Prothom Alo that firefighters had recovered four bodies from the burnt restaurant by 11:00 am. Five other injured people were rescued and admitted to Ukhiya Hospital. None of the victims has been identified.

However, all the casualties are believed to be tourists, as Patowar Tek Beach is a tourist destination. Several people said the fire may have originated from the stove in the resort's kitchen, but this has not yet been confirmed. he added.

Locals said the fire broke out at the resort, located beside the Marine Drive road, at around 7:30am. On receiving the news, firefighters arrived at the scene. Later, local residents, with police assistance, began efforts to bring the fire under control and rescue people.

Seven tourists are missing following the fire. They are believed to be trapped inside the resort. Firefighters are continuing rescue operations, while police are also at the scene. The cause of the fire was not immediately known.

item.title: US holds more secret talks with Myanmar's military-backed rulers in Tokyo, sources say
item.description:
MYANMAR-CONFLICT

The US and Myanmar's military-backed government held talks in Tokyo last week, people familiar with the matter said, their second meeting in a month as Washington steps up re-engagement with the generals it shunned after their 2021 coup.

Earlier talks in Myanmar's capital Naypyitaw in mid-September focused on securing the release of an American businessman and shutting down scam centers that target Americans, but could pave the way for broader discussions, including on Myanmar’s rare-earth mineral deposits, Reuters previously reported.

It was not immediately clear exactly what the two sides discussed at last week's talks, disclosed to Reuters by three people with knowledge of the engagement. The people, including one US official, all requested anonymity because of the sensitivity of the meeting.

US Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance again led the Tokyo talks, which involved more than a dozen US officials, one of the people said. Reuters could not establish who represented Myanmar.

A US official disputed that Vance is leading US policy toward Myanmar. "In coordination with other agencies, the State Department has a wide range of officials that lead on Burma policy," the US official said, using the country's former name.

The Trump administration says it engages with all ⁠groups in Myanmar on issues affecting US interests. A spokesperson for Myanmar's military-backed government did not respond to a request for comment.

Asked about its role in hosting the talks, Japan's Foreign Ministry said in an emailed statement it had been "communicating as necessary" with both sides but declined to comment on specific diplomatic exchanges.

Last month's meeting in Naypyitaw between Vance and Myanmar's coup leader-turned-president, Min Aung Hlaing, provided an opening for broader discussions, people familiar with those talks previously told Reuters. The quick return to the negotiating table in Tokyo suggests both sides are keen to keep the dialogue going.

A major focus of the US push is securing Myanmar's help in shutting down scam hubs that run romance and other frauds and have swindled Americans out of billions of dollars, the people said.

Researchers say many scam operations are based in areas controlled by army-backed militia, with some proceeds flowing to the military, raising doubts about whether Myanmar's leaders are serious about enforcement. Myanmar's military-backed government has said it is participating in a multinational effort to curb scam centres.

US officials have also discussed access to Myanmar's large deposits of heavy rare earths, which are used in products ranging from electric vehicles to wind turbines. US officials acknowledge significant obstacles: the deposits are largely located in territory controlled by ethnic armed groups fighting the military, while China, the main buyer of Myanmar rare earths, could balk at any US role.

The US last week lifted sanctions on the daughter of a Myanmar businessman accused of supporting the country's military, saying the move was part of a new approach to the country.

"This approach highlights the importance of pursuing dialogue with all groups involved in Burma’s civil war and commits to re-examining the range of tools the United States has historically leveraged to promote core interests in the country," the State Department said of the sanctions move.

Min Aung Hlaing remains under US sanctions for human rights abuses, including for his role in the coup and crushing a subsequent popular uprising, and the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims that Washington declared a genocide. The armed forces have killed thousands of people in airstrikes since the putsch, which sparked widespread civil war, the United Nations says.

The latest engagements in Japan show the Trump administration views Myanmar through a "purely transactionalist lens," said Hunter Marston, Southeast Asia director at the Lowy Institute, an Australian think tank.

"The critical minerals and rare earths that Myanmar holds are viewed as probably the chief strategic asset that Washington is interested in within Myanmar," Marston said.

Japan's role unclear

It is unclear whether Japan has any stake in the US-Myanmar talks beyond playing host, including for earlier talks in the Japanese capital in June, but there are signs that Tokyo is also moving to re-engage with Myanmar.

Japan's acting envoy to Myanmar met with the foreign minister of Myanmar's military-backed government earlier this month in their first known public engagement. Tokyo does not formally recognise the administration.

That meeting followed a September visit by Japanese ruling party lawmaker Hiromichi Watanabe to Naypyitaw, which he said was aimed at restarting bilateral cooperation and resuming development aid to Myanmar, according to the state-run Global New Light of Myanmar newspaper.

Japan's Foreign Ministry said the acting envoy raised issues such as protection for Japanese nationals and support for Japanese companies, while Watanabe's trip was in his capacity as an individual member of parliament and "does not in any way prejudge" the position of the government.

Watanabe told Reuters his trip was aimed at preparing the environment to normalise relations, though he acknowledged that barriers remained.

Japan condemned the military's 2021 overthrow of Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government but stopped short of joining the US and other Western governments in imposing sanctions on junta leaders and military-linked entities.

Tokyo was one of Myanmar's largest foreign investors, seeking to counter China's influence in one of Asia's last frontier markets. Unlike numerous Western firms, many Japanese companies remained despite the turmoil that followed the 2021 coup.

Around 300 Japanese companies still operate in Myanmar, down from more than 400 in 2020, according to Japan's trade promotion agency, JETRO.

item.title: Tanker hit off Saudi’s Gulf coast, crew evacuated
item.description:
A tanker was struck by an “unknown projectile” off Saudi Arabia’s Gulf coast, forcing the evacuation of its crew, a maritime monitoring agency said on Saturday.
The vessel was hit on Friday, 68 nautical miles off the coast of Jubail, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said, adding that “all crew are reported safe.”
Ships have regularly come under Iranian fire during the Middle East war, as Iran blockades the Strait of Hormuz -- the only exit route for oil and gas exports via the Gulf sea.
Vanguard, another maritime security agency, identified the ship as the Marshall Islands-flagged Safeen Principal crude oil tanker, saying it lost power and suffered an engine-room fire.
UKMTO later said that also on Friday, a ship in the same area was attacked by a rocket-propelled grenade, with the crew reported safe.
About one-fifth of global oil exports passed through Hormuz before the war began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28. Oil prices have soared during the war.

item.title: France faces day of cost-of-living protests
item.description:
French authorities detained dozens on Saturday at the start of nationwide protests against the cost of living, in what is likely to be a key indicator of the social climate heading toward elections to replace President Emmanuel Macron.
With just months to go before the two-round elections in April and May to choose Macron’s successor, the demonstrations follow weeks of high-school student blockades demanding better learning conditions.
These have at times turned into violent clashes, and sparked criticism from rights groups that the police have used disproportionate force in response.
The main Paris demonstration was to kick off at 2pm (1200 GMT) at the Republique square.
The country’s Yellow Vest movement, which eight years ago staged street protests against Macron’s government over planned fuel tax hikes, has called Saturday’s “yellow and youth” demonstrations.
It has appealed to teachers and students, workers, pensioners and farmers to take part in the protests on the first day of half-term holidays.
The protests geared up with a handful of gatherings nationwide on Saturday morning, AFP reporters said.
In the western city of Rennes, around 20 people set up a barricade using trash bins and large pallets on the outskirts of a shopping mall.
Christophe, a 47-year-old carpenter and former Yellow Vest protester who did not give his surname, said he was indignant after seeing what he viewed as police brutality against teenagers in recent weeks.
“We’ve reached the point where the repression is targeting our own children,” he told AFP.
In the southern city of Marseille, some protesters attacked a police building, an AFP photographer saw.
Demonstrators clashed with police -- who responded with tear gas -- and briefly blocked a main road with rubbish bins and scooters before officers cleared it.
“We’re here to protest the deplorable resources allocated to education and against police brutality,” said Aude, a masked student who did not give her surname.
In Paris, where the authorities have banned protests around government buildings, the Champs-Elysees shopping avenue and train stations, police detained around 60 people on Saturday morning.
Police officers asked passersby for ID outside the Saint-Lazare station, AFP reporters said.
Protesters in balaclavas in the morning threw projectiles and broke windows at the headquarters of the right-leaning television broadcaster CNews.
“It’s not just a Yellow Vest movement, it’s not just a student movement, it’s all the people who are rising up and that’s why those in power are afraid,” said Benjamin Ball, an activist working on a website for the demonstrations.
More than 600 demonstrations were planned across France, according to the website set up by organizers.
Around 45 percent of French people are worried about the cost of living and inflation, according to a survey of 2,000 people published earlier this month.
Macron on Friday evening called “for calm and respect.” In Brussels for European Union talks, he added the right to protest went hand in hand with “respect for people and property.”
The unrest has been seized upon by France’s far-left and far-right parties.
Jean-Luc Melenchon, leader of the far-left France Unbowed party, has backed the student protests and marched in one demonstration Tuesday supporting them.
Marine Le Pen, who leads in opinion polls for the presidential race, has positioned her National Rally party on the side of the police.

State reforms obstructed by power politics and bureaucratic clout: TIB
item.description:
Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB) stated in a statement today, Friday, that the potential for establishing an accountable government system and reforming the state, which emerged through the mass uprising in July, is being hindered by power politics and bureaucratic influence.

TIB pointed out that due to the interim government's lack of strategic planning and bold initiatives, as well as compromises with bureaucratic resistance, the foundation for state reform has not been established.

The implementation of constitutional amendments and the July National Charter after the 13th National Assembly elections has become dependent on the whims of the ruling coalition.

On the other hand, the opposition coalition is busy with partisan political interests rather than playing a supportive role in state reform for the public interest.

TIB's Executive Director, Iftekharuzzaman, mentioned that there was a commitment in the 31-point demand and the election manifesto to implement state reforms and the July National Charter word for word.

However, uncertainty has arisen over the reform process as the members of parliament from the winning party did not take the oath as members of the proposed Constitutional Reform Commission. According to him, the process of constitutional amendment, lawmaking, and institutional reform is now dependent on the inclinations of the ruling coalition.

Noting that the current government has turned many of the 133 ordinances issued by the interim government into law, TIB's Executive Director said that only those ordinances that strengthened the executive branch have been passed. On the other hand, ordinances assisting in establishing accountability have been repealed or suspended.

Iftekharuzzaman stated that the path to establishing an accountable government system is being obstructed by the collusion of power politics and bureaucratic forces. At the same time, practices of grabbing, extortion, and politicisation are making state reform and the implementation of the July Charter difficult with a "now it's our turn" mentality.

TIB has also raised questions about the government's role in ensuring the independence of the judiciary. The statement noted that by repealing the Supreme Court Secretariat (Amendment) Ordinance and the Supreme Court Judges Appointment Ordinance, the government has taken a stance opposed to state reform. Furthermore, by not converting the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) Amendment Ordinance into law with necessary amendments and reverting to the 2004 law, the opportunity to overcome the trust deficit in the commission has been obstructed.

TIB expressed concern about the National Human Rights Commission as well.

According to the organisation, repealing the ordinance related to the commission and enacting a new law is contrary to public aspirations for establishing an independent and effective commission and conflicted with international standards.

Moreover, by repealing the Disappearances Prevention and Remedy Ordinance, an opportunity has been created to protect agencies responsible for human rights violations.

TIB also criticised the move to make the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB) more powerful under a new identity instead of dissolving it. Additionally, the statement noted that although there is a consensus among political parties on forming an independent police commission, no initiatives have been taken in this regard.

Regarding the disclosure of assets by elected public representatives, Iftekharuzzaman said there was consensus on publishing the asset details of all elected public representatives within three months of assuming office and regularly updating them.

However, after the members of parliament were sworn in, there is no reflection of such directives or practices. These steps risk establishing an unaccountable power structure instead of ensuring accountability of the executive branch.

Iftekharuzzaman also questioned why the government and political parties are not learning from the consequences of turning the judiciary, law enforcement agencies, ACC, and National Human Rights Commission into partisan institutions during authoritarian regimes.

The TIB statement said that during the drafting of the July National Charter, an unprecedented political consensus emerged amidst Bangladesh's divided political culture.

The organisation called upon all political parties to demonstrate similar goodwill and wisdom to achieve the goal of state reform.

item.title: Bangladesh seeks details from Saudi Arabia on execution of 2 nationals
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam on Saturday said the government is yet to receive detailed official information from the Saudi authorities regarding the recent execution of a Bangladeshi man and a woman, stressing that such unfortunate news is not expected.
“We have yet to receive any official detailed information from the Saudi government,” she told reporters at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, noting that Bangladesh sent a letter to the Saudi government requesting detailed information.
Earlier, Saudi media reported that the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia executed the two Bangladeshis after they were convicted of committing “indecent acts” inside a mosque in the holy city of Mecca.
Quoting the Saudi Interior Ministry, Gulf News reported that the court imposed the sentences because of the seriousness of the offence, the violation of the sanctity of the mosque, and the circumstances in which the acts were committed.
The Saudi authorities identified the two Bangladeshis as Nazrul Islam Abdul Basir and Siti Akhtar.
“On October 14, we learned that two Bangladeshi nationals had been sentenced to death under Saudi Arabian law and that the executions had been carried out,” the state minister said, noting that neither the Ministry of Foreign Affairs nor the Bangladesh Mission in Saudi Arabia had been informed in advance.
“We wanted to know whatever we needed to know. Let the reply come. I will be able to let you know,” Shama said.
Upon learning of the incident, the Bangladesh Mission notified the Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment, sharing all the information it had gathered from Saudi authorities.
The state minister said the government sent a formal inquiry to ascertain the full details, including the identities of the individuals, their backgrounds in Bangladesh, and when they had originally arrived in Saudi Arabia for work.

item.title: Bangladesh urges UN action to end Israeli occupation
item.description:
Bangladesh has called for urgent international action to end Israeli occupation, illegal settlement expansion and human rights violations in Palestine, reaffirming its unwavering solidarity with the Palestinian people and their right to self-determination.
Bangladesh's Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Ambassador Irene Khan made the call while addressing the UN Security Council's open debate on "The Situation in the Middle East, including the Palestinian Question" in New York on Friday, according to a press release received here on Saturday.
Expressing grave concern over the humanitarian devastation in Gaza, she strongly condemned the continuing suffering of Palestinian civilians and escalating Israeli actions in the occupied Palestinian territories.
Ambassador Khan also voiced deep concern over increasing land confiscation, violence and illegal settlement expansion in the West Bank and Jerusalem.
"The deadlock in the Security Council has enabled Israel to operate with impunity," she said.
The Bangladesh envoy urged the Security Council to take decisive measures to halt annexation, forced displacement and human rights violations in the occupied Palestinian territories.
She stressed the need to ensure accountability for violations of international law and protect the fundamental rights of the Palestinian people.
Reaffirming Bangladesh's longstanding position on the Palestinian question, Khan said Dhaka remained firmly committed to supporting the Palestinian people's inalienable right to self-determination.
She also underscored the importance of ensuring uninterrupted humanitarian assistance to Palestinians and called for full respect for the mandate of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA).
The ambassador stressed that humanitarian agencies must be allowed to continue their operations to provide essential assistance to vulnerable Palestinian populations.
Turning to the broader Middle East situation, Khan condemned Israeli attacks and occupation in Syria and Lebanon, expressing concern over their implications for regional peace and stability.
She emphasized the need for an adequate United Nations presence in Lebanon and offered Bangladesh's support in this regard.
The Bangladesh envoy also strongly condemned the deadly Houthi attacks on airports in Saudi Arabia that caused civilian casualties, including among Bangladeshi migrant workers.
She expressed concern over the threats such attacks posed to civilian lives and regional security.
Reaffirming Bangladesh's commitment to promoting a Culture of Peace, Ambassador Khan urged all parties to exercise maximum restraint, protect civilians and uphold international humanitarian law.
She stressed the importance of collective international efforts to prevent further escalation and promote lasting peace and stability in the Middle East.

item.title: Metro rail's Motijheel to Kamalapur expected to open in July next year
item.description:
The much-anticipated extension of Metro Rail's MRT Line-6 from Motijheel to Kamalapur is expected to open for commercial operations in July next year.
“The overall physical progress of the civil construction work on the Motijheel-Kamalapur extension of MRT Line-6 has reached 84.85%,” Project Director of the Dhaka Mass Transit Development Project (MRT Line-6), Brigadier General (Retd) Md Abdul Wohab, told BSS here on Saturday.
He said mechanical, electrical and plumbing (MEP) works at Kamalapur station are underway, while equipment manufactured abroad will be installed soon after being brought into the country.
According to project details, electro-mechanical works on the extension have progressed by 58%, while construction of the 1.16-kilometre viaduct on the Motijheel-Kamalapur extension has been completed, and it has been handed over to Contract Package-7 (CP-07) for rail track installation.
The structural work on Kamalapur MRT Station has also been completed, while MEP and architectural works are underway and are expected to be finished by December 31, 2026.
Meanwhile, work on seven integrated electro-mechanical subsystems under CP-07 is progressing. These include electrical and track systems, signaling, automatic fare collection (AFC), platform screen doors (PSD), telecommunications, lifts and escalators.
The 21.26-kilometre MRT Line-6, extending from Uttara North to Kamalapur, is progressing towards completion. As of September 30, 2026, the physical progress of the Uttara North-Motijheel section stood at 99.67%, while civil construction work on the Motijheel-Kamalapur extension had reached 84.85%.
Once the final section becomes operational, MRT Line-6 will connect Uttara North (Diabari) directly to Kamalapur Railway Station, completing the full 21.26-kilometre route.
The line will have 17 stations, including major stops at Mirpur-10, Agargaon, Farmgate and Dhaka University.
The metro rail began operating on the Uttara–Agargaon section on December 28, 2022. The Agargaon–Motijheel section opened on November 4, 2023. Since the Motijheel section opened, the metro rail has become a vital transport link for Dhaka residents, serving thousands of commuters daily.
Under the current schedule, the first trains depart from Motijheel at 7am and Uttara North at 6:40am.
On average, more than 0.4 million passengers have travelled on the metro rail since its launch, while on September 10, over 0.5 million passengers travelled on the metro, according to project information.
Revenue from ticket sales is also increasing as passenger numbers grow.

item.title: IMF: 29% highly educated in Bangladesh remain unemployed
item.description:
Nearly 29% of highly educated youth in Bangladesh are unemployed.
On the other hand, nearly half of the highly educated employed population is engaged in professions where their educational qualifications and skills are not being properly utilized.
This information came to light in a report by the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
This picture was highlighted in the IMF's Regional Economic Outlook: Asia and Pacific report, released at a press conference held on October 15 at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center in Bangkok, Thailand.
According to the report, the overall youth unemployment rate in Bangladesh is 12% to 13%.
However, the situation is even more alarming for highly educated youth.
Due to a mismatch between the quality of education and the demands of the labor market, many young people are unable to find jobs corresponding to their qualifications.
The IMF report stated that nearly 50% of highly educated working professionals in Bangladesh are working in low-tier occupations relative to their qualifications.
A major reason for this problem is the gap between skills acquired from educational institutions and the requirements of employers.
Consequently, many are forced to engage in work that is inconsistent with their training and educational qualifications, which is also limiting the country's economic productivity.
The report also cited the dominance of the informal sector as a labor market weakness.
Many workers employed in agriculture and other informal sectors lack formal employment contracts, job security, and opportunities for career advancement.
As a result, conventional unemployment statistics do not fully reflect the actual uncertainty of employment.
According to IMF projections, the working-age population aged 15 to 64 in Bangladesh will increase by about 10%-12% between 2025 and 2035.
To translate this demographic potential into economic strength, creating productive and quality employment is essential.
The organization particularly emphasized expanding new job opportunities in the manufacturing and service sectors.
The report also highlighted the impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on the labor market in Asia.
Recruitment demand in occupations highly exposed to AI has decreased by about 10% compared to less affected professions.
However, the demand for workers with specialized AI-related skills is increasing.
The IMF warned that without aligning workers' skills with technological shifts, Bangladesh's employment crisis could worsen.
To address this situation, adopting strategies focused on skill development, enhancing labor market capacity, and creating future-ready employment is crucial.
